# 8-Week Reminder Calendar (Relative to Move Day)

Set Move Day as your anchor date and count backward. I've suggested days and times, but shift them to fit your schedules. Copy each **Calendar Text** line directly into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, or whatever you use. Add the responsible person as an attendee or tag so you both see it.

---

## WEEK 8 (56–50 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Send written lease termination notice to landlord |
| Mon | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Request 3 moving quotes — call or schedule video surveys |
| Tue | 12:00 PM | M | MOVE: Get 2–3 vehicle shipping quotes (if shipping) |
| Wed | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Review moving budget spreadsheet together — set spending limits |
| Thu | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Book vet visit for dog — records, vaccines, health check |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | M | MOVE: Price DIY truck rentals (U-Haul, Penske, Budget) |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Research Oregon neighborhoods and start rental search |

## WEEK 7 (49–43 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Choose mover or DIY — read contracts before signing |
| Mon | 11:00 AM | M | MOVE: Book mover or reserve truck/container — pay deposit |
| Tue | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Schedule car maintenance (oil, tires, brakes, battery) |
| Wed | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Apply for Oregon rental — submit applications |
| Thu | 12:00 PM | M | MOVE: Book vehicle shipping if applicable — confirm pickup window |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Call Oregon internet provider — schedule install for arrival week |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Start declutter — garage and storage areas today |

## WEEK 6 (42–36 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Sign Oregon lease or confirm housing — save docs to Move folder |
| Tue | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Plan driving route — book 2–3 dog-friendly hotels along the way |
| Wed | 12:00 PM | J | MOVE: Order packing supplies — boxes, tape, bubble wrap, markers |
| Thu | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Declutter session — closets and guest room |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | P | MOVE: Notify employer of move date — ask about relocation help |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Book temporary housing in Oregon if needed (dog-friendly) |

## WEEK 5 (35–29 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: File USPS change of address at usps.com (set forward date) |
| Mon | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Schedule Ohio utility shutoffs for day after move |
| Tue | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Schedule Oregon utility start dates — electric, gas, water |
| Wed | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Begin packing non-essential rooms — books, decor, off-season clothes |
| Thu | 12:00 PM | M | MOVE: Gather all important documents into one folder (see doc list) |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Notify banks, credit cards, and insurers of upcoming address change |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Declutter and donate session — schedule charity pickup if needed |

## WEEK 4 (28–22 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | M | MOVE: Call auto insurer — confirm coverage in Oregon, update policy |
| Tue | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Pack guest room, storage, and garage — label every box by room |
| Wed | 12:00 PM | J | MOVE: Cancel or transfer subscriptions — gym, newspaper, meal kits |
| Thu | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Research Oregon DMV requirements — license, registration, emissions |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | M | MOVE: Find new vet near Oregon home — call to set up first visit |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Sell or give away remaining unwanted items — post online today |

## WEEK 3 (21–15 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Confirm mover date, crew size, arrival window, and payment method |
| Mon | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Confirm vehicle shipping pickup date and carrier contact |
| Tue | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Pack kitchen non-essentials — keep one pot, one pan, basic utensils |
| Wed | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Pack living room — art, books, electronics (photograph serial numbers) |
| Thu | 12:00 PM | M | MOVE: Order new dog ID tag with Oregon phone number or address |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Confirm Ohio final utility reads and Oregon utility start dates |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Assemble dog travel kit — food, bowls, leash, meds, blanket, toy |

## WEEK 2 (14–8 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Pack bedrooms — leave out 3 days of clothes and bedding per person |
| Tue | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Pack bathrooms — keep one towel, toiletries bag, and meds per person |
| Wed | 12:00 PM | M | MOVE: Get renter's insurance active for Oregon move-in date |
| Thu | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Photograph all valuables and serial numbers — save to phone and USB |
| Fri | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Pack "Last Out / First In" box — sheets, towels, toilet paper, snacks, tools |
| Sat | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Final donation and trash run — nothing left to decide on |
| Sun | 6:00 PM | M | MOVE: Prep car emergency kit and load moving-day essentials into car |

## WEEK 1 (7–1 days out)

| Day | Time | Who | Calendar Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon (7 days) | 9:00 AM | J | MOVE: Final packing — only daily essentials remain unpacked |
| Tue (6 days) | 10:00 AM | M | MOVE: Fill car with gas — check tires, oil, wipers, coolant |
| Wed (5 days) | 6:00 PM | J | MOVE: Defrost and clean fridge/freezer — donate perishable food |
| Thu (4 days) | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Confirm mover arrival time and payment — have cash tip ready |
| Fri (3 days) | 9:00 AM | M | MOVE: Confirm dog overnight stops are still booked and dog-friendly |
| Sat (2 days) | 10:00 AM | J | MOVE: Final walkthrough cleaning — photograph every room |
| Sun (1 day) | 8:00 PM | J | MOVE: Set alarms — lay out tomorrow's clothes, keys, documents, phone chargers |

---
---

# MOVING DAY ESSENTIALS — One Page for the Car

*Print this. Tape it to the dashboard or keep it in the glove box.*

---

**DOCUMENTS (one folder or pouch)**
- [ ] Driver's licenses and passports
- [ ] Vehicle title, registration, insurance card
- [ ] Lease / closing docs (both homes)
- [ ] Moving contract and Bill of Lading
- [ ] Vehicle shipping receipt and carrier number
- [ ] Dog: rabies cert, vaccine records, microchip number, vet contact
- [ ] Prescriptions and medical info
- [ ] Birth certificates, Social Security cards
- [ ] Insurance policy numbers (auto, renters, health)

**PERSONAL ESSENTIALS**
- [ ] Phone chargers and power bank
- [ ] Laptop and charger
- [ ] Wallets, keys (old and new home)
- [ ] 2–3 changes of clothes per person
- [ ] Toiletries bag (toothbrush, deodorant, contacts, meds)
- [ ] Glasses or contacts and backup pair
- [ ] Pillows and one blanket or sleeping bag per person
- [ ] Snacks and water bottles
- [ ] Cash (for tips, tolls, emergencies)

**DOG KIT**
- [ ] Leash, collar, harness
- [ ] Food (pre-portioned for each day), treats
- [ ] Collapsible water bowl and water bottle
- [ ] Poop bags
- [ ] Medications and calming aids
- [ ] Favorite toy and familiar blanket
- [ ] Crate or car barrier/seatbelt harness
- [ ] Vet records copy (in document folder)
- [ ] New ID tag with current phone number

**CAR EMERGENCY KIT**
- [ ] Jumper cables or jump pack
- [ ] Tire pressure gauge
- [ ] Flashlight and batteries
- [ ] First aid kit
- [ ] Spare tire, jack, lug wrench (confirm they're in the car)
- [ ] Roadside assistance number saved in phone
- [ ] Paper maps or downloaded offline maps (cell dead zones in Wyoming/Idaho)

**CLEANING AND TOOLS (for both ends)**
- [ ] Multi-tool or basic screwdriver set
- [ ] Box cutter and tape
- [ ] Paper towels, trash bags, all-purpose cleaner
- [ ] Toilet paper

**BEFORE YOU DRIVE AWAY**
- [ ] Final walkthrough — every room, closet, cabinet, garage
- [ ] Photos/video of empty unit
- [ ] Meter readings photographed
- [ ] Keys, remotes, fobs returned — get receipt
- [ ] Mover has your phone number and Oregon address
- [ ] Dog is secure, water is accessible, car is cool

---

*Safe travels. You've got this.*

turns.text:
# Room-by-Room Packing & Declutter Plan

**Before you start:** Set up a simple labeling system. Every box gets a label with three things: a room code, a sequential number, and a priority tag. Write it on two sides and the top with a thick marker.

**Room codes:** KIT (kitchen), LR (living room), BR1 (primary bedroom), BR2 (second bedroom/office), BA1 (primary bath), BA2 (second bath), GAR (garage), ATT (attic), BSM (basement), OUT (outdoor), LAU (laundry), CLO (hall closet/coat closet).

**Format:** KIT-04 / FRAGILE / OPEN FIRST — meaning kitchen box number 4, fragile contents, unpack this one immediately.

**Priority tags:** OPEN FIRST (essentials for night one), FRAGILE, HEAVY (keep small and under 50 lbs), DONATE, and SELL.

Keep a running inventory on your phone. A shared Google Sheet or Apple Note works fine: box number, room, short contents list, priority tag. Photograph the inside of each box before taping it shut. It takes five seconds and saves twenty minutes of searching later.

---

## KITCHEN — Pack weeks 3–2, finish week 1

**Estimated time:** 6–10 hours total across multiple sessions. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] Pull everything out of cabinets one section at a time. Group into keep, donate, toss.
- [ ] Purge duplicates: how many spatulas, can openers, and mugs do you actually use? Keep the ones you reach for. The rest go.
- [ ] Toss expired spices, food, and anything sticky or stale. Check the backs of cabinets.
- [ ] Donate small appliances you haven't used in a year (bread maker, fondue pot, spare blender).
- [ ] Recycle takeout containers, mismatched lids, and chipped dishes.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Entertaining and holiday items, baking supplies you won't use, cookbooks, decorative items, bar tools, vases.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Most dishes, glasses, pots, pans, and small appliances. Keep one pot, one pan, one cutting board, one knife, two plates, two bowls, two mugs, two forks/knives/spoons, a can opener, and a dish towel unpacked until moving day.
- [ ] **Last (day before or morning of):** The survival set above, cleaning supplies, trash bags, paper towels.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap each plate individually in packing paper. Stack plates vertically on edge like records — they're stronger that way and less likely to crack.
- [ ] Wrap glasses and mugs with packing paper stuffed inside the cup. Nest them upside down in cells or in a box with cardboard dividers.
- [ ] Put a 2-inch cushion of crumpled paper on the bottom and top of every fragile box.
- [ ] Never let fragile items touch each other or the box walls.
- [ ] Use dish towels and oven mitts as padding — they're free and they're coming with you anyway.
- [ ] Mark FRAGILE and THIS SIDE UP on two sides and the top. Draw an arrow.

---

## LIVING ROOM — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 4–6 hours. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Sort books: keep favorites, donate the rest to a Little Free Library or used bookstore. Books are the heaviest thing you own per cubic foot.
- [ ] Assess decor honestly. If you haven't noticed it in six months, donate it.
- [ ] Check media: DVDs, CDs, and games you've replaced digitally can go.
- [ ] Test electronics. If it's broken and you haven't fixed it yet, you won't fix it after the move.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Books (small boxes — never fill a large box with books), DVDs/games, wall art, decorative objects, photo frames, candles.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Lamps (remove bulbs and shades, wrap separately), electronics (see fragile tips), throw pillows and blankets, curtains and rods.
- [ ] **Last (week 1):** TV, gaming console, router/modem, streaming devices. Photograph the cable setup on the back of your TV and router before unplugging.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap framed art and mirrors in bubble wrap, then sandwich between two pieces of cardboard taped together. Mark GLASS.
- [ ] If you have original boxes for electronics, use them. If not, wrap in bubble wrap and pack snugly so nothing shifts.
- [ ] Zip cables into labeled bags (write what they connect to). Tape the bag to the device or put it in the same box.
- [ ] Remove batteries from remotes to prevent corrosion.
- [ ] Lamp shades dent easily. Wrap in paper, never in bubble wrap (it leaves marks). Pack in a separate box, top only, nothing on top of them.

---

## PRIMARY BEDROOM (BR1) — Pack weeks 2–1

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Clothing: try the reverse-hanger trick if you have a few weeks — turn all hangers backward, and anything you don't wear stays turned and gets donated.
- [ ] Shoes: if they're worn out or uncomfortable, they go.
- [ ] Nightstand junk drawer: sort, toss, keep.
- [ ] Under the bed: pull everything out. Be honest.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Off-season clothing, formal wear, shoes you won't need. Use wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes if your mover offers them, or leave clothes on hangers and drape a trash bag over a bundle with a hole for the hooks.
- [ ] **Second (end of week 2):** Most dresser contents, extra bedding, decorative pillows, nightstand items.
- [ ] **Last (morning of move):** The sheets you slept on, the pillow you used, the clothes you're wearing tomorrow, and the phone charger. These go in the car, not the truck.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Jewelry: carry it with you in the car. Use a small ziplock or travel case.
- [ ] Use clothing (socks, t-shirts) to wrap small fragile items like picture frames. It saves paper and packs two things at once.

---

## SECOND BEDROOM / OFFICE (BR2) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours. **Who:** P

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Shred old documents you no longer need (see the document list for what to keep).
- [ ] Recycle old magazines, catalogs, and junk mail piles.
- [ ] Sort office supplies — donate excess pens, binders, and notebooks to a school or thrift store.
- [ ] Old tech (chargers for devices you don't own, dead hard drives, tangled mystery cables): e-waste recycling.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Books, files you're keeping, craft supplies, decorative items, guest bedding.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Desk contents, office supplies, monitor, printer. Photograph cable setups.
- [ ] **Last (week 1):** Laptop and work essentials. If you're working remotely up to the move, this may be the very last thing packed. Keep it in the car.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Monitors: wrap the screen face with a soft cloth, then bubble wrap. Pack upright, never flat, and mark which side is the screen.
- [ ] Hard drives and backup drives: carry in the car. They're irreplaceable.

---

## BATHROOMS (BA1, BA2) — Pack week 1

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours total. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (30 min per bathroom)**

- [ ] Check expiration dates on medications, sunscreen, and first aid supplies. Toss expired items safely (many pharmacies accept old meds).
- [ ] Discard nearly empty bottles, dried-out products, and hotel toiletries you'll never use.
- [ ] Old towels that are threadbare: donate to an animal shelter, they always need them.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Guest towels, extra supplies, medicine cabinet overflow, cleaning products you won't need again.
- [ ] **Second (day before):** Most toiletries, towels, bath mat, shower curtain.
- [ ] **Last (morning of):** Toothbrushes, deodorant, face wash, prescription meds, one towel per person. These go in your toiletry bag in the car.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Put caps on liquids and seal them in individual ziplock bags in case they leak. Group the bags in one box.
- [ ] Mirrors: wrap and pack like art (see living room).

---

## LAUNDRY ROOM — Pack week 1

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours. **Who:** P

**Declutter (20 min)**

- [ ] Toss nearly empty detergent bottles and stained rags.
- [ ] Donate surplus cleaning supplies rather than moving them 2,400 miles.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Iron, ironing board, drying rack, extra supplies.
- [ ] **Second (day before):** Do a final load of laundry. Pack detergent, hamper, and remaining supplies.
- [ ] **Last:** Leave the washer and dryer doors open overnight after the final load to prevent mildew (if you own them and they're staying, wipe them down).

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Seal all liquids in ziplock bags. Transport upright.

---

## HALL CLOSETS / COAT CLOSETS (CLO) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per closet. **Who:** J

**Declutter (30 min per closet)**

- [ ] Off-season coats you haven't worn in two years: donate.
- [ ] Board games missing pieces, old umbrellas, random bags: toss or donate.
- [ ] Luggage: empty it, check every pocket, then use it as a packing container for soft items.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Seasonal gear, luggage (packed with soft items inside), board games, extra linens.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Coats, shoes, vacuum, miscellaneous.
- [ ] **Last:** Keep one coat per person accessible if traveling through mountain weather (you will be).

---

## GARAGE (GAR) — Pack weeks 4–3

**Estimated time:** 4–8 hours depending on volume. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (2–3 hours — this is usually the biggest purge)**

- [ ] Sort tools: keep one good set, donate or sell duplicates. A cross-country move is not worth it for a rusty rake.
- [ ] Chemicals, paint, propane, fertilizer, pesticides: movers cannot transport these and you should not put them in a moving truck. Dispose of them at your county hazardous waste facility or give them to a neighbor.
- [ ] Old furniture, broken items, and "I'll fix it someday" projects: be ruthless. Sell, donate, or curb alert.
- [ ] Sports equipment nobody uses: donate.
- [ ] Holiday decorations: keep only what you love. Donate the rest.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 4):** Holiday decorations, seasonal items, rarely used tools.
- [ ] **Second (week 3):** Remaining tools, workbench contents, bikes, sports gear. Disassemble what you can.
- [ ] **Last (week 2):** Items you use regularly — lawn equipment (if bringing it), car supplies, step ladder.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap power tool blades and sharp edges in cardboard secured with tape.
- [ ] Drain fuel from all gas-powered equipment (mower, trimmer, chainsaw). Movers and truck rental companies prohibit fuel.

---

## ATTIC (ATT) — Pack weeks 5–4

**Estimated time:** 2–6 hours depending on what's up there. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] If you haven't opened a box since the last move, seriously consider donating it unopened or at least opening it and deciding quickly.
- [ ] Check for water damage and pest damage. Damaged items are not worth moving.
- [ ] Sentimental items: keep what matters, photograph the rest and let it go.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 5):** Since attic items are by definition not in daily use, pack everything early. Re-box items in deteriorated boxes.
- [ ] **Last:** Nothing should remain in the attic by week 3.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Old photos and documents: pack flat in a sealed plastic bin to protect from moisture during transport. Carry irreplaceable photos in the car.

---

## BASEMENT (BSM) — Pack weeks 5–3

**Estimated time:** 3–6 hours. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] Same rules as attic: if it's been down there untouched for years, question its value.
- [ ] Check for mold or mildew on stored items. Don't bring it to the new home.
- [ ] Old paint cans, solvents, and chemicals: hazardous waste disposal, same as garage.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 5):** Storage items, seasonal decor, archived boxes.
- [ ] **Second (week 4):** Furniture, exercise equipment (disassemble what you can and bag the hardware in labeled ziplock bags taped to the item).
- [ ] **Last (week 3):** Anything you're still using regularly.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap exercise equipment screens and panels in bubble wrap. Tape loose cables to the frame.

---

## OUTDOOR SPACES (OUT) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 2–4 hours. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Decide what patio furniture is worth moving. Resin chairs cost less to replace than to ship.
- [ ] Garden tools: keep the good ones, donate the rest.
- [ ] Potted plants: movers generally will not transport live plants across state lines (and Oregon has agricultural restrictions). Give them to friends or neighbors. Research Oregon's plant import rules if you want to bring something specific.
- [ ] Hoses, sprinklers, and yard chemicals: usually cheaper to replace than to move.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Decor, string lights, bird feeders, small garden tools.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Patio furniture (disassemble if possible), grill (clean it, remove the propane tank, do not transport propane).
- [ ] **Last:** Door mats, welcome signs, house numbers (if yours).

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Ceramic pots break easily. Wrap in bubble wrap and pack in boxes with crumpled paper. If the pot isn't special, leave it.

---

## GENERAL PACKING RULES

**The heavy-light rule:** Heavy items (books, tools, cans) go in small boxes. Light items (linens, pillows, clothes) go in large boxes. Never make a box heavier than you can comfortably lift.

**The 50-pound rule:** No box should exceed roughly 50 lbs. Your back, your movers, and your boxes will all thank you.

**Fill every box completely.** Half-empty boxes collapse when stacked. Use packing paper, towels, or clothing to fill gaps.

**Tape matters.** Use quality packing tape, not masking tape or duct tape. Tape the bottom of every box with an H-pattern (one strip down the center seam, one strip across each edge).

**One room per box.** Don't mix rooms. It makes unpacking chaotic.

**Color coding (optional upgrade):** Buy colored dot stickers — one color per room

# DELIVERABLE 2B: Declutter-for-Sale Plan (One Page)

**Responsibility: P** leads listings and communication. **M** handles photos and staging. **J** for pricing decisions.

## Where to Sell

**Facebook Marketplace** is the strongest platform for furniture, appliances, and household goods in most Ohio markets. It's free to list, has local reach, and buyers expect to pick up. **Craigslist** still works for tools, electronics, and niche items but has a smaller audience than it used to. **OfferUp** is a decent backup, especially in suburban areas. **Nextdoor** is good for small items and "curb alert" free-stuff posts. **Mercari or eBay** are worth it only for items worth $40+ that are easy to ship (electronics, collectibles, brand-name goods), because they take fees and require shipping logistics you don't have time for right now.

**Recommended default:** List everything on Facebook Marketplace first. Cross-post to Craigslist if it doesn't sell in 3 days.

## Pricing Guidance

The goal is speed, not maximum profit. You're on a 4–6 week sell-off window. Price to move, not to negotiate.

A reasonable starting point for used household goods in good condition is roughly 25–40% of what it costs new. For furniture, 30–50% of retail if it's in good shape and from a recognizable brand, and 15–25% if it's flat-pack or heavily used. For electronics, check the same item's "sold" listings on eBay or Facebook to see what people actually paid, not what others are asking. For free stuff, post it on your curb with a "FREE" sign and a Nextdoor post. It will disappear in hours.

**The two-week rule:** If it hasn't sold in a week, drop the price by 25–30%. If it still hasn't sold after two weeks, donate it, give it away, or leave it curbside. You do not have time for a third week.

## Sample Listings

**Version 1: Quick Sell (priced to go fast)**

Title: `IKEA KALLAX shelf 4x2 — white — $30 OBO — must pick up by Saturday`

Description: `IKEA KALLAX 4x2 shelf unit in white. Good condition, some minor scratches on top. We're moving and need it gone this week. $30 or best offer. Pickup only — [your neighborhood or cross streets]. Available evenings and Saturday morning. Cash or Venmo.`

**Version 2: Better Price (for items worth more patience)**

Title: `West Elm Mid-Century Media Console — Acorn — 56" — $275`

Description: `West Elm mid-century media console in Acorn finish, 56 inches wide. Bought in 2022 for $600. Excellent condition — no scratches, stains, or damage. Holds a 55" TV comfortably. Solid wood legs, two cabinets with adjustable shelves. We're relocating out of state; available for pickup in [neighborhood] anytime in the next two weeks. I can help load if you bring a truck or SUV. $275 firm for the first week; after that I'll consider offers. Cash, Venmo, or Zelle.`

## Photo Tips

Take photos in daylight, not under overhead lamps. Open the curtains or move the item near a window. Clear clutter from the background — buyers are looking at your item, but a messy room makes everything look worse. Shoot one wide shot showing the full item, one close-up of the brand label or any notable detail, and one close-up of any flaws (scratches, stains). Showing flaws builds trust and prevents time-wasting arguments at pickup. Shoot at the item's level, not looking down at it. Five photos is enough for most items.

## Pickup and Safety

Meet buyers at your front door or driveway, not inside the house. Daytime pickups only. If the item is small and you're uncomfortable with a home address, meet at a well-lit public spot (many police stations have designated safe-trade zones in the parking lot). Tell someone in your household when a buyer is coming and roughly when. Cash is king, but Venmo and Zelle work. Don't accept personal checks. If a buyer asks you to ship something, says they'll send a courier, or offers to overpay with a cashier's check, it's a scam — ignore and move on. Don't hold items without a deposit; "I'll come tomorrow" often means never. First person with cash in hand wins.

## Declutter-for-Sale Timeline

Weeks 6–5: List the big-ticket items (furniture, appliances, electronics) while you still have time to wait for a fair price. Weeks 4–3: Drop prices on anything unsold, list medium items (kitchen gear, tools, decor). Weeks 2–1: Everything remaining either gets donated, given away on Nextdoor/curb alert, or goes in the trash. Do not let unsold items delay your packing. The last week is for packing and cleaning, not negotiating with buyers.

# Ohio → Oregon Vehicle & DMV Action Plan

**Important caveat:** DMV rules, fees, and timelines change. Everything below reflects information current as of early-to-mid 2025. Verify details at the official Oregon DMV site (oregon.gov/odot/dmv) and Ohio BMV site before you act. Call ahead to confirm document requirements, especially for financed vehicles, because individual DMV offices sometimes ask for additional paperwork.

---

## TIMELINE AT A GLANCE

Oregon law generally requires new residents to get an Oregon driver's license and register their vehicles within 30 days of establishing residency. "Establishing residency" typically means the date you move in, start working, or enroll kids in school — whichever comes first. In practice, you want to start the process in your first two weeks so you aren't scrambling at the deadline.

| When | What | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Before you leave Ohio | Gather documents, contact lienholder, do NOT cancel Ohio registration yet | M |
| Days 1–3 in Oregon | Settle in, locate nearest DMV, book appointments online | M |
| Days 4–10 | Get Oregon driver's licenses (both of you) | M and P separately |
| Days 7–14 | Get emissions test if required in your county | M |
| Days 10–20 | Register vehicle(s) and title in Oregon | M |
| Days 20–30 | Confirm everything is complete, update insurance, cancel Ohio registration and return plates | M |

---

## STEP 1: BEFORE YOU LEAVE OHIO

**Who:** M leads, P gathers their own license documents.

**Timeline:** Weeks 3–1 before move.

**1a. Gather documents for each vehicle**

- [ ] Ohio certificate of title. If you have a paper title in hand with no lien, you're set. Bring the original.
- [ ] Current Ohio registration card.
- [ ] Proof of insurance (your current policy is fine for now as long as it covers you in Oregon — call your insurer to confirm).
- [ ] Odometer reading (write it down; you'll need it for the Oregon title application).

**1b. If the vehicle is financed or leased**

This is the step most people underestimate. If there's a lien on the title, the lienholder (bank, credit union, or lease company) holds the title or is listed on it. Oregon DMV needs the title or proof of lien to register.

- [ ] Call your lienholder now, at least 2–3 weeks before the move. Tell them you're moving to Oregon and need to register the vehicle there.
- [ ] Ask the lienholder to send the title directly to the Oregon DMV, or ask them to send you a letter of authorization (sometimes called a "letter of lien" or "lienholder authorization") that Oregon DMV can accept in lieu of the physical title.
- [ ] Some lienholders will send an electronic lien (ELT) directly to Oregon. Ask if they participate in Oregon's ELT program.
- [ ] If the lienholder mails a physical title, have them send it to your new Oregon address or to the Oregon DMV office you plan to visit. Do not have it sent to your old Ohio address after you've left.
- [ ] Get the lienholder's exact legal name and address as it appears on the title — Oregon DMV will need this.
- [ ] If you're leasing, contact the leasing company. Some lease agreements restrict out-of-state registration. Get written confirmation that you're allowed to register in Oregon.

**1c. Contact your auto insurance company**

- [ ] Tell them your move date and new address.
- [ ] Confirm your policy covers you in Oregon effective on your arrival date.
- [ ] Ask about updating the policy to Oregon after you register. Some insurers handle this as a simple address change; others require you to start a new policy with Oregon-specific coverage.
- [ ] Get a new insurance card or digital proof showing Oregon coverage. You'll need proof of insurance at the Oregon DMV.

**1d. Do NOT cancel Ohio registration or return Ohio plates yet**

You need valid registration to legally drive the car to Oregon. Keep Ohio plates on the vehicle until Oregon plates are in hand. Cancel Ohio registration after Oregon registration is complete.

---

## STEP 2: DAYS 1–3 IN OREGON — SET UP APPOINTMENTS

**Who:** M

Oregon DMV offices are appointment-preferred. Walk-ins are possible but wait times can be very long, especially in the Portland metro area.

- [ ] Go to oregon.gov/odot/dmv and book appointments for driver's license and vehicle registration. You can sometimes combine them into one visit, but it depends on the office. Book the earliest slots available.
- [ ] Identify which DMV office serves your area. Major offices include Portland (multiple locations), Salem, Eugene, Bend, and Medford.
- [ ] Check the specific office's hours and whether they handle titling (most full-service offices do, but some smaller ones have limited services).

---

## STEP 3: DAYS 4–10 — GET OREGON DRIVER'S LICENSES

**Who:** M and P each do this individually. You can go together but each person completes their own application.

**What to bring (each person)**

- [ ] Your current valid Ohio driver's license.
- [ ] Proof of legal presence (U.S. passport, birth certificate, or permanent resident card). If you want a Real ID–compliant license, you'll need one of these plus proof of Social Security number (SSN card or W-2) and two proofs of Oregon residency (lease agreement, utility bill in your name, bank statement with Oregon address). Check the Real ID document requirements on the Oregon DMV site for the current list.
- [ ] If you don't need Real ID, the requirements may be simpler, but Oregon has been issuing Real ID–compliant licenses by default. Verify what your specific situation requires.
- [ ] Payment (see fees below).

**What happens at the DMV**

Oregon generally does not require a written knowledge test if you hold a valid license from another state, but policies can vary and this may have changed. Check the DMV site or call ahead to confirm. You will not need a driving test. You will get a vision screening. You will get a new photo taken. You'll surrender your Ohio license (they'll punch a hole in it and may let you keep it, or they may keep it).

**Fees (ballpark, verify current amounts)**

Oregon driver's license for a standard license is typically around $40–$60 for an 8-year license. Real ID–compliant licenses may cost slightly more. Check the current fee schedule on the Oregon DMV site.

---

## STEP 4: DAYS 7–14 — EMISSIONS TESTING (IF REQUIRED)

**Who:** M

This is the step that depends entirely on where in Oregon you're living. Oregon's DEQ (Department of Environmental Quality) requires emissions testing in specific areas. Here's the breakdown by major region:

**Portland Metro (Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties)**

Required. This is the most common scenario for new residents. You need a DEQ emissions test before you can register a vehicle that is new to Oregon (meaning it wasn't previously registered here). The test is called a "Clean Air Station" test. Stations are located throughout the metro area. The test is a tailpipe or OBD-II scan depending on the vehicle's year. Cost is approximately $25 as of recent years. You can find station locations and hours at oregon.gov/deq. Some stations accept walk-ins; some require appointments. Go early in the day for shorter lines.

**Eugene / Springfield (Lane County, parts of)**

Required in the Eugene-Springfield urban growth boundary. Same DEQ test, same approximate cost. Fewer stations than Portland, so book early or go at off-peak times.

**Medford / Ashland (Jackson County, parts of)**

Required in the Medford-Ashland area and Rogue Valley. Same DEQ test.

**Bend (Deschutes County)**

Not required. Bend and Central Oregon are outside the DEQ testing area. No emissions test needed to register.

**Salem, Corvallis, coast cities, rural Oregon**

Not required in most of these areas. If you're unsure, check the DEQ boundary maps on the DEQ website or call them.

**What to bring to the emissions test**

- [ ] The vehicle.
- [ ] Your Ohio registration (to prove it's your car).
- [ ] Payment (cash or card, approximately $25).
- [ ] You'll receive a certificate or receipt. Keep it — you'll need it at the DMV for registration.

**Common issue:** If your car fails the emissions test, you'll need to get it repaired and retested before you can register. If you suspect your car might have an emissions issue (check engine light on, old catalytic converter), consider getting it checked before the move.

---

## STEP 5: DAYS 10–20 — REGISTER AND TITLE THE VEHICLE IN OREGON

**Who:** M

**What to bring**

- [ ] Oregon driver's license (get this first, it makes everything smoother).
- [ ] Ohio certificate of title (original). If financed, bring the lienholder authorization letter, or confirm the lienholder has sent the title or ELT to Oregon DMV.
- [ ] Current Ohio registration card.
- [ ] Proof of Oregon insurance (updated card or printout showing the vehicle, your name, and Oregon address).
- [ ] DEQ emissions certificate (if your county requires it).
- [ ] Odometer disclosure (the DMV form will ask for this; just know your mileage).
- [ ] VIN — the DMV may do a VIN inspection at the counter or may require one done separately. For most standard passenger vehicles transferring from another state with a clean title, this is handled at the counter. Call ahead to confirm.
- [ ] Payment for fees (see below).

**Fees (ballpark, verify current amounts)**

Oregon vehicle fees include a title fee (typically around $80–$100), registration fee (typically around $120–$175 for a standard passenger vehicle for a 2-year registration), and plate fees (around $25 for standard plates). There may also be a county-specific fee and a parks fee. Total out-the-door for titling and registering one standard vehicle is commonly in the $200–$350 range, but it varies based on vehicle type and county. Electric and hybrid vehicles may have additional fees. Check oregon.gov/odot/dmv for the current fee calculator.

**What happens**

You'll fill out a title and registration application. The DMV will process the Ohio title, issue an Oregon title (mailed to you or your lienholder), and issue Oregon plates and registration. You'll get plates and a registration card that day in most cases. Put the new plates on before you drive away.

**If the vehicle is financed**

Oregon DMV will list the lienholder on the new Oregon title. The title will be sent directly to the lienholder or held electronically. This is standard and your lienholder should expect it if you've contacted them in advance.

---

## STEP 6: DAYS 20–30 — CLOSE OUT OHIO

**Who:** M

- [ ] Cancel your Ohio vehicle registration. You can do this by mailing your Ohio plates back to the Ohio BMV or by visiting an Ohio BMV deputy registrar office (which you obviously can't do from Oregon). The standard method is to mail the plates to: Ohio BMV, P.O. Box 16520, Columbus, OH 43216-6520, with a note requesting cancellation and including your name, Ohio registration number, and new state of registration. Check the Ohio BMV site for the current process and address.
- [ ] Request a refund of any unused registration period if Ohio allows prorated refunds (they sometimes do, depending on how much time was left). Check with Ohio BMV.
- [ ] Confirm your auto insurance has been fully updated to Oregon. The old Ohio policy should be replaced, not running in parallel. You don't want to pay for both.
- [ ] Keep a copy of your Ohio registration cancellation confirmation for your records.
- [ ] Update your insurance company with the new Oregon plate numbers and registration info.

---

## QUICK REFERENCE: DOCUMENTS CHECKLIST FOR DMV VISITS

Print this and bring everything. It's better to have a document you don't need than to make a second trip.

**For driver's license (each person)**

- [ ] Current Ohio license
- [ ] U.S. passport or birth certificate
- [ ] Social Security card or W-2 (for Real ID)
- [ ] Two proofs of Oregon address (lease, utility bill, bank statement)
- [ ] Payment

**For vehicle registration (each vehicle)**

- [ ] Oregon driver's license
- [ ] Ohio title (original) or lienholder authorization
- [ ] Ohio registration card
- [ ] Oregon insurance proof
- [ ] DEQ emissions certificate (if applicable)
- [ ] Odometer reading
- [ ] Payment

---

## FEES SUMMARY (BALLPARK PER VEHICLE)

| Item | Estimated Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Oregon driver's license | $40–$60 each | Per person, 8-year license |
| DEQ emissions test | ~$25 | Only if in a required area |
| Oregon title fee | $80–$100 | Per vehicle |
| Oregon registration (2-year) | $120–$175 | Varies by vehicle type |
| Plate fee | ~$25 | Standard plates |
| County/parks fees | $10–$30 | Varies |
| **Total per vehicle** | **$275–$430** | Rough range |
| **Total for 2 licenses + 1 vehicle** | **$355–$550** | Rough range |

---

## COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID

**Don't let the 30-day window expire.** Oregon can cite you for driving with out-of-state registration beyond the residency grace period. It's not heavily enforced, but if you get pulled over or have an accident, it becomes a problem.

**Don't cancel Ohio registration before Oregon plates are on the car.** You'd be driving an unregistered vehicle, which creates insurance and legal issues.

**Don't forget the lienholder lead time.** Banks are slow. Start the conversation 2–3 weeks before the move, not after you arrive.

**Don't skip the emissions test if you're in a required area.** The DMV will not register the vehicle without it.

**Don't assume your insurance auto-transfers.** Call your insurer. Some require a new policy for a new state. If you have a gap in coverage, Oregon DMV won't register the car, and you're driving uninsured.
